title: Back to the Moon, On to Mars
summary: In April 2026, four astronauts flew all the way around the Moon, farther from Earth than any people ever before. Robots from China, India, Japan and private companies are landing on the Moon too, hunting for ice hidden in dark craters. Next comes a Moon base, and one day maybe Mars, and the first people to walk there could be kids reading this right now.

sections.heading: Artemis, Twin Sister of Apollo
paragraphs: In Greek myth, Apollo had a twin sister: Artemis, goddess of the Moon. So when NASA planned a new program to send people back to the Moon, more than fifty years after Apollo, it chose her name. The program's goal is not just to plant flags and footprints, as in 1969, but to learn how to stay: to build a long-lasting human presence on and around the Moon, and to use it as practice for going to Mars.

Artemis has two main pieces of hardware built by NASA. The first is the Space Launch System, or SLS, a giant rocket about 98 m tall, a little shorter than the Saturn V but more powerful at liftoff. Its orange core stage burns liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen in four RS-25 engines, the same type that once powered the Space Shuttle, and some of these very engines actually flew on Shuttle missions. Two white solid rocket boosters, also descended from the Shuttle's boosters, provide most of the push in the first two minutes. The second piece is Orion, a cone-shaped crew capsule a bit like a much bigger Apollo command module, with room for four astronauts. Orion's service module, which supplies power, air, water and the main engine, is built in Europe for the European Space Agency.

Artemis I was the test with no crew aboard. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida in the early hours of 16 November 2022, lighting up the night sky. Orion flew out to the Moon, swung within about 130 km of the lunar surface, and then went into a wide, looping orbit far beyond it. At its farthest point, it was about 432,000 km from Earth, farther than any spacecraft built to carry humans had ever gone. Instead of astronauts, the seats held mannequins fitted with sensors to measure vibration and radiation, and a plush Snoopy toy floated in the cabin as a zero-gravity indicator, showing when the capsule was in free fall.

After about 25 days, Orion splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 11 December 2022, exactly fifty years after Apollo 17 landed on the Moon. The mission was a success, but engineers found something surprising when they inspected the capsule: pieces of the outer layer of its heat shield had cracked and broken away in an unexpected way during the fiery return. Months of tests followed. NASA decided to keep the shield for the next mission but to change Orion's path back into the atmosphere, so the capsule would spend less time in the conditions that caused the damage.

sections.heading: Artemis II: Four People Around the Moon
paragraphs: On 1 April 2026, after several delays caused by the heat shield studies and by leaks of liquid hydrogen during fuelling tests, the SLS rocket roared off Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center, the same pad used by Apollo 10 and many Space Shuttles. Inside the Orion capsule, which the crew had named Integrity, were four astronauts. Reid Wiseman, from NASA, was the commander. Victor Glover, from NASA, was the pilot. Christina Koch, from NASA, and Jeremy Hansen, from the Canadian Space Agency, were mission specialists. Koch became the first woman to travel to the Moon, Glover the first Black astronaut to do so, and Hansen the first person from outside the United States to fly beyond low Earth orbit.

Artemis II did not land on the Moon, and it did not go into orbit around it. It followed what is called a free-return trajectory: a path shaped like a stretched figure eight, where the Moon's gravity bends the spacecraft around and flings it back toward Earth even without a big engine burn. Apollo 13's crew used a path like this to get home safely in 1970. For Artemis II, it was chosen as a safety measure for the first crewed test. First, though, the crew spent about a day circling Earth, checking that Orion's life support, controls and communications worked, before firing toward the Moon.

On 6 April 2026, Orion swept around the far side of the Moon. The crew looked down on parts of the far side that no human eyes had ever seen directly and took hundreds of photographs. They also saw a total solar eclipse from space, as the Moon passed in front of the Sun from their point of view; Glover said afterwards that it had amazed all of them. During the flyby, the crew reached a distance of about 406,771 km (252,756 miles) from Earth, the farthest any humans have ever travelled. The record they broke had stood since Apollo 13 in April 1970.

Then came the long fall home. Orion hit the top of the atmosphere at about 11 km per second, more than 39,000 km per hour, the fastest any crew had re-entered since the Apollo era. After a fiery few minutes and a planned radio blackout, its parachutes opened, and on 10 April 2026 Integrity splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California, where the US Navy ship USS John P. Murtha was waiting. The whole mission lasted 9 days, 1 hour and 32 minutes. It was not perfectly smooth: the crew dealt with some valve problems and even a misbehaving toilet. But all four astronauts came home safely, and humans had travelled to the Moon for the first time in more than half a century.

What comes next? Space plans change often, and Artemis is no exception. In early 2026, NASA announced a big reshuffle. Under the new plan, Artemis III, which had been meant to be the first landing, would instead become a test mission in Earth orbit, aimed for 2027, where astronauts in Orion would practise meeting up with the new commercial Moon landers being built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. The first attempts to land astronauts near the Moon's south pole were moved to later missions, aimed for around 2028. These are targets, not promises. Each lander still has to be tested, and huge new systems almost always take longer than planned. Meanwhile, China has announced its own goal of landing astronauts on the Moon by around 2030, with a new rocket, a new crew spacecraft and a lander. Whichever mission comes first, a new chapter of Moon exploration has clearly begun.

sections.heading: A Crowd on the Moon
paragraphs: Between 1976 and 2013, no spacecraft made a soft landing on the Moon at all. Today the Moon is busy again, and much of the action comes from countries other than the United States and Russia.

China has carried out a remarkable step-by-step program named after Chang'e, the Moon goddess in Chinese legend. Chang'e 3 landed in 2013 with a small rover called Yutu, meaning Jade Rabbit, the goddess's companion. Then, on 3 January 2019, Chang'e 4 did something nobody had done before: it made a soft landing on the far side of the Moon, in Von Kármán crater. Because the Moon blocks radio signals from the far side, China first placed a relay satellite called Queqiao, meaning Magpie Bridge, far beyond the Moon, so the lander could talk to Earth through it. Its rover, Yutu-2, kept driving for years, far longer than planned.

In December 2020, Chang'e 5 landed on the near side, scooped and drilled about 1.7 kg of soil and rock, launched it back into lunar orbit, and returned it to Earth, the first lunar samples brought home since the Soviet Luna 24 in 1976. The samples turned out to include some of the youngest volcanic rocks ever collected from the Moon. In 2024, Chang'e 6 went one step further. It launched on 3 May, landed on 1 June inside the Apollo basin on the far side, and on 25 June its capsule landed in Inner Mongolia carrying about 1.9 kg of material, the first samples ever collected from the Moon's far side.

India's turn came after a disappointment. In 2019, the lander of Chandrayaan-2 crashed during its final descent. The Indian Space Research Organisation, ISRO, studied what went wrong, strengthened the lander's legs, widened its landing zone and improved its software. Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023, and on 23 August 2023 its lander, Vikram, touched down gently at about 69 degrees south, far closer to the south pole than any earlier landing. India became the fourth country to make a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China. The small rover, Pragyan, rolled down a ramp and drove about 100 m, and its instruments confirmed sulfur in the lunar soil. Only days earlier, Russia's Luna 25, also heading for the south polar region, had crashed after an engine problem.

More landers followed. Japan's SLIM spacecraft landed in January 2024 within about 100 m of its target, a remarkable feat of precision, although it ended up tipped on its nose; it still worked and sent back pictures. In February 2024, a lander called Odysseus, built by the American company Intuitive Machines, became the first privately built spacecraft to land on the Moon, though it also tipped over. In March 2025, Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost lander touched down upright and carried out its planned mission successfully, the first fully successful landing by a private company. Landing on the Moon is still hard, and several private landers have crashed. But each attempt, successful or not, teaches engineers something new, just as in the early days of the space race.

sections.heading: Treasure in the Dark
paragraphs: Why are so many missions heading for the Moon's south pole? The answer is a substance you drank today: water.

Earth's axis is tilted, which gives us seasons. The Moon's axis is tilted only about 1.5 degrees, so at its poles the Sun always hangs low on the horizon, like a sunset that never ends. The floors of some deep craters near the poles have not seen sunlight for perhaps billions of years. Measurements from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter show that some of these permanently shadowed craters are colder than minus 200 degrees Celsius, among the coldest places ever measured in the solar system. Any water molecules that drift into such a cold trap, perhaps delivered by comets or created by the solar wind, freeze and stay there.

For years scientists suspected ice was there. Then, on 9 October 2009, NASA deliberately crashed the spent upper stage of a rocket into a shadowed crater called Cabeus, near the south pole. A small spacecraft named LCROSS flew through the cloud of debris thrown up by the impact and detected water in it, before crashing in turn. Instruments on India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter, including one built by NASA, had also found signs of water on the lunar surface, and in 2018 scientists reported direct evidence of surface ice inside shadowed craters at both poles.

Water on the Moon would be worth far more than gold, because it is so heavy and expensive to launch from Earth. Astronauts could melt and clean it for drinking and for growing plants. Using electricity, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen could fill astronauts' air tanks. And hydrogen and oxygen, chilled into liquids, are exactly the propellants used by many powerful rocket engines. A Moon base that could make its own fuel could become a kind of filling station in space.

The south pole has another advantage: some high crater rims, such as parts of the rim of Shackleton crater, are lit by the Sun most of the time, which would be useful for solar power. Being next to both near-constant sunlight and frozen water makes these places some of the most valuable real estate in the solar system, which is exactly why the questions in Part 19 about who may use lunar resources matter so much. Scientists still do not know how much ice there is, how pure it is or how hard it will be to dig out of soil so cold. Finding out is one of the main jobs of the coming missions.

sections.heading: The Long Road to Mars
paragraphs: The Moon is about three days away. Mars is a completely different challenge. Depending on where the two planets are in their orbits, Mars is between about 55 million and 400 million km from Earth. With today's rockets, the trip takes around seven months each way, and launch windows open only about every 26 months, when the planets line up well. A crew might have to wait on Mars for more than a year before the next good window home. A full round trip could last two to three years.

Radiation is one of the biggest dangers. On Earth, our magnetic field and thick atmosphere shield us from energetic particles from the Sun and from exploding stars far away. In deep space, there is no such shield. During its trip to Mars in 2011 and 2012, the Curiosity rover carried an instrument that measured radiation inside its spacecraft. Scientists calculated that astronauts on a typical round trip would receive a radiation dose of about 0.66 sieverts from the journey alone, more than many space agencies' career limits for astronauts. Engineers are studying better shielding, using water tanks or food supplies as walls, and storm shelters where a crew could hide during a solar storm.

The human body also changes in weightlessness. As Part 16 explained, astronauts lose bone and muscle, which is why they exercise every day on the space station. Some also have changes in their eyesight. After seven months of floating, Mars astronauts would have to step out onto a planet with about 38% of Earth's gravity and immediately start working. Their minds matter too. Between 2010 and 2011, six men lived for 520 days in a sealed mock spaceship in Moscow in an experiment called Mars-500, to learn how a crew copes with isolation, boredom and a delay in talking to home. Real astronauts on Mars would wait up to about 20 minutes for a message to reach Earth, and as long again for the reply, so they would have to solve emergencies on their own.

They would also need food, water and air for years. Astronauts on the space station have already grown and eaten fresh food: in August 2015, a crew tasted red romaine lettuce grown in a small plant chamber called Veggie. On Mars itself, a small experiment called MOXIE aboard the Perseverance rover proved that oxygen can be made from the planet's thin carbon dioxide air. Over 16 runs between 2021 and 2023, it produced 122 grams of oxygen, about as much as a small dog breathes in ten hours. That is tiny, but it showed the idea works. A full-sized version could make oxygen for breathing and for the fuel of the rocket home.

Then there is the landing. Mars has an atmosphere only about one percent as thick as Earth's, too thin for parachutes alone to slow down a heavy ship, but thick enough to create dangerous heat on the way in. The heaviest thing ever landed on Mars so far is Perseverance, which weighs about one tonne. A ship carrying people, supplies and a rocket to return home might weigh dozens of tonnes. It would probably have to fire powerful engines downward while still flying faster than sound, a technique the reusable rockets of Part 18 have practised in Earth's atmosphere. SpaceX hopes its giant Starship could one day carry crews and cargo to Mars, and NASA and other agencies are studying their own designs. No one can yet give a reliable date for the first human landing on Mars; it is a goal, not a schedule.

sections.heading: New Engines for Long Journeys
paragraphs: Chemical rockets, which burn fuel with an oxidizer, have carried every human into space. They push hard, but they use up their propellant very quickly. For long journeys, engineers are testing other kinds of engines.

One is the ion engine. Instead of burning anything, it uses electricity, often from solar panels, to strip electrons off atoms of a gas such as xenon. The atoms become electrically charged ions, and a strong electric field flings them out of the back at about 30 to 40 km per second, roughly ten times faster than the exhaust of a chemical rocket. The push is incredibly gentle: the ion engines on NASA's Dawn spacecraft pushed about as hard as the weight of a single sheet of paper resting on your hand. But they can run for months or years without stopping, and in the emptiness of space that tiny push adds up.

Dawn launched on 27 September 2007. Using its ion engines for a total of more than five years of thrusting, it became the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth and the Moon: first the giant asteroid Vesta in 2011 and 2012, then the dwarf planet Ceres from 2015 to 2018, where it discovered bright patches of salt. Its ion engines changed its speed by about 11 km per second in total, more than any spacecraft had achieved with its own engines before. Earlier, in 1998, NASA's Deep Space 1 had been the first deep-space mission to rely on ion propulsion, and ion thrusters now help keep many communications satellites in place.

Ion engines are too gentle to carry a heavy crewed ship quickly to Mars on their own, so engineers are also looking at nuclear power. In a nuclear thermal rocket, a small reactor would heat hydrogen to extremely high temperatures and blast it out of a nozzle, about twice as efficiently as the best chemical engines. The United States built and ground-tested such engines in the 1960s in a program called NERVA, but none ever flew. A faster trip would mean less time exposed to radiation and weightlessness, which is why the idea keeps coming back. Nuclear power is not new in space: Voyager, Curiosity and Perseverance all get their electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium. In 2018, NASA also successfully tested a small fission reactor called Kilopower in Nevada, designed to one day power a base on the Moon or Mars.

Some ideas use no fuel at all. In 2010, Japan's IKAROS spacecraft unfurled a solar sail, a thin sheet thinner than a human hair, and was pushed along by the gentle pressure of sunlight itself, on its way past Venus. Engineers are also studying ways to make propellant on other worlds, so ships do not have to carry everything from Earth. The rockets of the future may look very different from the fire arrows of the past, but they will still obey the same rule Newton wrote down in 1687: push something one way, and you go the other.

sections.heading: One Long Relay Race
paragraphs: Step back and look at the whole story you have just read. It is not the tale of one genius or one country. It is more like a relay race lasting a thousand years, where each runner carried the baton a little further and then passed it on.

It began with Chinese alchemists who stumbled on gunpowder while searching for medicines, and soldiers who discovered that a tube of burning powder could push an arrow by itself. Rockets spread to the Mongols, the Islamic world and Europe. In India, Tipu Sultan's iron-cased rockets impressed the British so much that William Congreve copied and improved them, and their red glare entered a national anthem. Isaac Newton explained why any of it worked: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

Then came the dreamers. Jules Verne imagined a journey to the Moon. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a deaf schoolteacher in a small Russian town, worked out the mathematics of rockets and imagined space stations and multi-stage rocket trains. Robert Goddard, alone in a snowy field in Massachusetts in 1926, launched the first liquid-fuel rocket. Hermann Oberth's books inspired rocket clubs full of young enthusiasts.

The darkest chapter came next, when rockets became weapons of war, built by forced labourers, and the V-2 became the first human-made object to reach space. After the war, Sergei Korolev in the Soviet Union and Wernher von Braun in the United States led rival teams. Korolev's R-7 launched Sputnik and then Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space. Von Braun's Saturn V carried Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and ten other astronauts to walk on the Moon. Behind them stood hundreds of thousands of people: engineers, seamstresses who sewed the spacesuits, mathematicians such as Katherine Johnson, and programmers such as Margaret Hamilton's team.

Space stations taught humans to live in orbit, and the International Space Station turned old rivals into partners. Robot explorers visited every planet. Then companies learned to land rockets and fly them again, making launches far cheaper. And in April 2026, four astronauts from two countries looped around the Moon, carrying the baton further from Earth than anyone had ever been. Every step built on the steps before it, and people from China, India, the Middle East, Europe, Russia, America, Japan and many other places all ran a leg of the race.

sections.heading: Your Countdown
paragraphs: Now think about this. If people do reach Mars in the 2030s or 2040s, the astronauts who make that trip are probably not famous yet. Many of them are still in school. Some might be about your age. The engineers who design their ship, the doctors who keep them healthy, the scientists who decide where they will land and the programmers who write the software that steers them home may be sitting in classrooms right now, wondering what they will be when they grow up.

You do not have to be an astronaut to be part of space exploration. Remember that Tsiolkovsky taught himself from library books, that Goddard was laughed at by a newspaper, that Katherine Johnson's careful arithmetic helped bring astronauts home, and that Mars rovers are driven by teams of scientists who never leave Earth. Curiosity, patience and the courage to keep trying after failures have mattered as much as any rocket engine. Space needs builders, writers, artists, doctors, lawyers, farmers who can grow food in strange places, and people who ask hard questions about safety and fairness.

So imagine it. You are strapped into a seat, looking up through a small window at a deep blue sky. Beneath you, a rocket hums and creaks as icy propellant boils off. A calm voice in your headset begins to count.

Ten. Nine. Eight. Somewhere far below, a fire arrow from a thousand years ago whooshes into the air. Seven. Six. Newton writes down his third law by candlelight. Five. Four. A deaf schoolteacher in Kaluga fills a notebook with equations. Three. Two. A small rocket leaps from a cabbage field in Massachusetts, and Gagarin shouts that it is time to go. One. The engines roar, the whole ship shakes, and you are pressed back into your seat as the sky turns from blue to black.
Liftoff. The next chapter of this story is yours.

deepDive: Why go to the Moon to reach Mars, and why do engineers obsess over lunar ice? The answer is the rocket equation from Part 4. A rocket's total possible change in speed, called delta-v, depends on its exhaust speed multiplied by the natural logarithm of its fuelled mass divided by its empty mass. That logarithm is brutal: to double your delta-v you must square your mass ratio. Reaching low Earth orbit takes about 9.4 km/s of delta-v once gravity and air drag losses are included, which is why rockets launched from Earth are mostly propellant. Escaping the Moon's surface, by contrast, takes only about 2.4 km/s, because the Moon has about one-sixth of Earth's surface gravity and no air. So propellant made on the Moon would be far cheaper, in energy, to deliver into space than the same propellant lifted from Earth. Whether that advantage outweighs the cost of building mining and processing plants on the Moon is a major open question, and estimates vary widely. Artemis has its own debates. The SLS rocket is largely expendable: each one is thrown away after a single launch. In 2022, NASA's Office of Inspector General estimated that each of the first four Artemis launches would cost about 4.1 billion US dollars for the SLS, Orion and ground systems, a figure critics argue is too high to support frequent missions. Supporters reply that SLS was the only system available to send Orion and its crew directly toward the Moon. The landers chosen by NASA, SpaceX's Starship-based lander and Blue Origin's Blue Moon, both depend on refuelling in orbit, transferring very cold propellant between spacecraft in weightlessness, something never yet done at that scale. Starship's lunar lander is expected to need many tanker launches to fill up, which is one reason schedules are uncertain. For Mars, the main competition is between chemical propulsion with refuelling and nuclear propulsion. A nuclear thermal rocket with an exhaust speed of about 9 km/s, double that of the best hydrogen-oxygen engines, could shorten trips and reduce radiation dose, but it raises questions about safety, testing and cost. Nobody yet knows which approach will carry the first crew to Mars.
funFact: On their April 2026 flight around the Moon, the Artemis II astronauts travelled 406,771 km from Earth, breaking a distance record set by the Apollo 13 crew in 1970.
